1303.title: The Udasis
1303.hook: an ascetic order tracing itself to Sri Chand, which cared for many gurdwaras in hard times
1303.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the Udasis as caretakers of many gurdwaras in the years when Khalsa Sikhs were hunted, and hold a range of views about the order's place in the panth today.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sampardaa, a tradition handed on, and your line was many streams, one guru. Today the first stream: an order that kept the doors open.

A family leaves home in a hurry, and a neighbor promises to look after the house. Months go by, then years. The neighbor waters the plants, sweeps the step, opens the windows on hot days so the place can breathe. When the family finally comes back, the lamp in the front room is still lit. Nobody stood guard with a weapon. Somebody just kept showing up. The Sikh panth tells a story with that shape about its own shrines, and the neighbors in it belong to an order you met in year three, through the Guru's son.
screen: `A FAMILY LEAVES IN A HURRY.` → `A NEIGHBOR KEEPS THE HOUSE.` → `THE LAMP STILL LIT.`

segments.voice: The Udasis are an order of renunciants. They trace themselves to Baba Sri Chand, Guru Nanak's elder son, who chose a celibate life of meditation, as year three told. Udasi teachers kept Guru Nanak's hymns at the center of their devotion, and tradition remembers the later Gurus and Sri Chand meeting with respect. Year three also walked through the years when Khalsa Sikhs were hunted, living in forests and on horseback, unable to stay safely near their own shrines. Tradition says that in those years Udasi caretakers looked after many gurdwaras. They didn't wear the Khalsa's outward form, so they could stay where Khalsa Sikhs could not. They kept the doors open, the lamps lit, and the Guru's word read. There's a second chapter. Tradition also remembers that, much later, at some shrines the hereditary caretakers grew wealthy and careless, and a reform movement brought those shrines back under the panth's own care. That story comes on another day; hold both chapters together, and let neither erase the other. Last, a line from Guru Nanak close to the word udasi, which carries the sense of being detached. In the conversation with the Siddhas, the yogis of the mountains, he gives a picture of detachment, in paraphrase: like a lotus that floats untouched by the water, like a duck that swims the stream and stays dry. The Udasis chose a renunciant's road to seek that freedom. In the hard years, their freedom from house and household left them free to keep the Guru's house.
screen: `AN ORDER TRACED TO BABA SRI CHAND.` · `THE HARD YEARS: KHALSA SIKHS HUNTED.` · `UDASIS KEPT THE LAMPS LIT.` · `THE LOTUS UNTOUCHED BY THE WATER.` · then, large: `KEEPERS IN HARD TIMES.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who quietly kept something going, a grandparent who held the family's prayers, a caretaker at a place of worship, and see what they kept and what might have been lost without them. Breathe in their name and breathe out a little thanks, and if you pray, rest on Waheguru.
Udasi. A renunciant order tracing itself to Baba Sri Chand. Tradition says Udasi caretakers kept many gurdwaras open when Khalsa Sikhs could not. Today's word.
Your line: keepers in hard times. Sometimes faithfulness looks like a lamp that is simply never let go out. Day thirteen-oh-three, done.

1304.title: Udasi places today
1304.hook: Udasi centers still stand in Punjab and beyond
1304.howItsDone: Udasi deras and akharas still stand in Punjab and beyond; visitors find Guru Nanak's hymns honored there, alongside Baba Sri Chand's memory and renunciant customs of their own.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Udasis, the order traced to Baba Sri Chand, and your line was keepers in hard times. Today, where they still are.

Through a low gate, there's a courtyard with a big old tree in the middle and a wide platform under it. In one corner, a fire pit with ash that someone tends every day. A low building with a painted doorway, and inside, on a raised seat, the Guru's word, wrapped in cloth. A man with long uncut hair and saffron cloth sweeps the floor before the visitors arrive. This is not a scene from an old painting. Places like this stand today.
screen: `A COURTYARD, A TREE, A FIRE PIT.` → `THE GURU'S WORD ON A RAISED SEAT.` → `NOT AN OLD PAINTING.`

segments.voice: Udasi centers go by a few names. A dera is a seat or settlement, where a teacher and his followers live. An akhara is a larger house of an order, with its own rules and leaders. Udasi deras and akharas still stand in Punjab, and beyond it. Tradition says Udasi teachers carried Guru Nanak's word far from Punjab, that some of their places sit along the great rivers of north India, where they join the vast gatherings of renunciants of many orders, and that others stand across the border, in what is now Pakistan. Inside, the details differ from place to place. Udasi places are known for keeping Guru Nanak's hymns at the center and honoring Baba Sri Chand. Some also keep practices from the wider world of Indian renunciants: the ash, the fire, the saffron. So a visitor may find something familiar and something different in the same courtyard. Sikhs hold a range of views about the Udasis today: some see a branch of the panth with roots in the Guru's own family, some a separate order with its own path, and others simply honor what they kept. This path describes; it doesn't decide. A line from the Japji fits any of these places. Guru Nanak describes the earth set among nights and seasons, days and dates, wind and water, and in paraphrase, he calls it a dharamsal: a place set up for practicing what is right. Sikh tradition remembers dharamsal as an early name for a place of worship. The Japji makes the whole earth one. Udasi places are small rooms in that big one, still standing.
screen: `DERA: A SEAT. AKHARA: A HOUSE.` · `IN PUNJAB, AND BEYOND IT.` · `FAMILIAR AND DIFFERENT, ONE COURTYARD.` · `THE EARTH AS A DHARAMSAL.` · then, large: `STILL STANDING.`

1305.title: The Nirmalas
1305.hook: scholars who, tradition says, were sent to study Sanskrit learning in Benares
1305.howItsDone: Nirmala scholars, who trace their order to students Guru Gobind Singh sent to Benares, teach and explain Gurbani; their deras still train students in reading and exposition.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Udasi places, deras and akharas in Punjab and beyond, and your line was still standing. Today, a road east, and a different kind of order.

Why would a Guru send his Sikhs away to study under teachers of another tradition? Follow the road east, toward the holy city on the Ganges. A few young Sikhs walk it with bundles on their backs, heading for teachers who may never have taught a Sikh before. They'll sit on the floor with students of another tradition, learn a difficult old language, memorize grammar until their heads ache, and read books in a script that's new to them. Tradition says Guru Gobind Singh sent them. The order that traces itself to those students is today's word.
screen: `A ROAD EAST, TO THE GANGES.` → `STUDENTS FROM ANOTHER TRADITION.` → `WHY WOULD A GURU SEND THEM?`

segments.voice: The story first, as tradition tells it. Guru Gobind Singh wanted Sikhs who could read the learning of the classical Indian schools for themselves: Sanskrit grammar, philosophy, the old texts learned men of his day quoted in their arguments. So, tradition says, he sent a small band of Sikhs to Benares, the city on the Ganges known for that learning. They came back as scholars, and the Nirmalas trace their order to them. Some accounts add names, a disguise, a teacher who at first refused them; the accounts differ, so today keeps only the shape. Next, the name. Nirmal is a word the Gurus use in their hymns. It means spotless, without stain, and they say it of the Name, of the mind made clear, of God. An order of scholars called itself by that word: the pure ones. Then, what learning is for. Guru Nanak has a short line in Raag Asa that the Nirmalas could have carried as a motto. In paraphrase: when learning is reflected upon, it becomes a kindness to others. Not learning to win arguments or to stand above people; learning thought through until it can help someone. Last, what they became. Nirmalas are remembered as teachers and preachers who explained the Gurus' hymns, drawing on the language of the scholars of their day. Some Sikhs value that bridge; some ask how much the borrowed language shaped the reading. Both questions are fair, and tomorrow looks at the explaining itself. A Guru who thought study was worth a long walk, and an order named for a spotless one.
screen: `TRADITION: SENT TO BENARES TO STUDY.` · `NIRMAL: SPOTLESS, WITHOUT STAIN.` · `LEARNING THAT HELPS OTHERS.` · `A BRIDGE, AND A FAIR QUESTION.` · then, large: `THE SCHOLARS.`

Nirmala. The pure ones: an order of Sikh scholars who, tradition says, trace themselves to students Guru Gobind Singh sent to Benares. Today's word.

1306.title: Nirmala learning
1306.hook: Nirmala scholars wrote commentaries explaining Gurbani
1306.howItsDone: Sikhs study Gurbani with teekas, written line-by-line commentaries, and katha, spoken explanation in the gurdwara; Nirmala scholars are among those who wrote and taught them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Nirmalas, the pure ones who studied in Benares, and your line was the scholars. Today, what their explaining looks like.

Two people read the same text message. Sounds good. One hears a happy yes. The other hears a tired, flat, fine, whatever. Same two words, two meanings, and the difference lives in something the words don't show. Old texts can do this too, Gurbani among them. A single word can lean two ways. So, for a long time, people have sat down with the Guru's lines and written out, slowly, what each one means. A scholar's explanation like that has a name, and Nirmala scholars wrote them.
screen: `SOUNDS GOOD: A YES, OR A SIGH?` → `ONE WORD CAN LEAN TWO WAYS.` → `SO SOMEONE WRITES IT OUT.`

segments.voice: The name is teeka: a commentary that walks through a text line by line. A teeka sets out the Guru's line, then the meaning of its words, then what the line is doing, and sometimes other ways to read it. Nirmala scholars wrote teekas and gave spoken explanations called katha, and students of Gurbani have learned from them. Here's the kind of question they worked on. The Japji's first step opens with a line built on the word soch. In paraphrase: by soch, it cannot be reached, even if one does soch a hundred thousand times. Soch can mean thinking; read that way, you can't think your way to God, however hard you think. But soch can also mean ritual cleansing, the bath and washing some held made a person pure; read that way, outward washing, however often, can't make the mind clean. Some readers hear it one way, some the other, and some hold both at once. Notice the link to yesterday's word, nirmal, without stain: either reading is about what actually makes a person clear. A careful teeka is honest when a word is hard, and lists the readings instead of hiding the choice. And it never replaces the Guru's line. The line stays on top; the explanation sits underneath. Readers can disagree with a teeka; that's allowed, and part of the tradition. The point of explaining is to send the reader back to the line with better ears.
screen: `TEEKA: A LINE-BY-LINE COMMENTARY.` · `SOCH: THINKING, OR WASHING?` · `A CAREFUL TEEKA LISTS THE READINGS.` · `THE LINE STAYS ON TOP.` · then, large: `EXPLAINED.`

segments.voice: Hold the Japji's line in mind: by soch, it cannot be reached. On one breath hear it as thinking, you can't think your way there; on the next, as washing, outward cleaning can't clean the mind. Go back and forth slowly, and let both readings stand.
Nirmala learning. Teekas and katha: scholars walking line by line through Gurbani, listing the readings, and keeping the Guru's line on top. Today's word.

1307.title: The Sevapanthis
1307.hook: followers of Bhai Kanhaiya, devoted to quiet service
1307.howItsDone: Sevapanthis, who trace their community to Bhai Kanhaiya, are remembered for serving travelers and the sick and for living by their own work; seva in the langar and the shoe room is part of everyday Sikh life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nirmala learning, teekas and katha with the line on top, and your line was explained. Today, a stream known less for words than for work.

At the end of a big event, the speakers get the applause and the photos. Then the hall empties, and a few people stay behind. They stack the chairs, wipe the tables, carry the bins out to the curb in the dark. Nobody films that part. In year one you met Bhai Kanhaiya, the water carrier on the battlefield who, the story says, saw his Guru's face in every wounded man. That was one day of his life. Today is about what came after him: people who made the stay-behind part their whole way of life.
screen: `THE SPEAKERS GET THE APPLAUSE.` → `A FEW STAY TO STACK THE CHAIRS.` → `AFTER BHAI KANHAIYA.`

segments.voice: The word is Sevapanthi: one who walks the path of seva, selfless service. Tradition says Bhai Kanhaiya's companions and followers formed a community around his way, and that community still exists. Tradition remembers three things about them. First, service is the center, not a side activity. Sevapanthis are remembered for running places where travelers could rest, drink and eat, and for tending the sick, without asking who anyone was. Second, they lived by their own work. Tradition says they didn't go begging for alms and earned their bread with their hands; serving others while asking nothing of them was the point. Third, quietness: they're remembered less for great deeds with names attached than for steady work over a long time. In Sri Raag, Guru Nanak gives a short line on seva. In paraphrase: do seva in this world, and you will find a place to sit in the Lord's court. Notice where the service happens: in this world, among people, in kitchens and on roads. And notice the reward: not applause, a seat, the way a tired traveler finds one at a Sevapanthi rest stop. Some Sikhs hear echoes of this in the langar, and in the shoe room at the gurdwara, where volunteers polish strangers' shoes. The Sevapanthis took that common Sikh practice and made it the name of their path. Not service as a break from real life; service as the real life, with the rest fitted in around it.
screen: `SEVAPANTHI: THE PATH OF SEVA.` · `REST, WATER AND FOOD FOR ANYONE.` · `BREAD EARNED BY THEIR OWN HANDS.` · `SRI RAAG: SERVE HERE, A SEAT THERE.` · then, large: `SERVICE FIRST.`

1308.title: The Nihang dals
1308.hook: blue-clad orders keeping the martial traditions and their own customs
1308.howItsDone: Nihang dals process with the nagara drum and the Nishan Sahib flag in front, notably at festivals such as Hola Mohalla, and keep horses, weapons training and their own customs in their camps.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sevapanthis, service at the center and bread earned by their own hands. Your line was service first. Today, a stream you hear before you see.

Boom. Boom. Boom. You hear it before you see anything: a big kettle drum, struck slow and heavy, carried on horseback or on a cart at the head of a line. Behind it, a tall triangular flag on a pole. Behind the flag, riders and walkers in deep blue, steel at their belts and in their turbans. Year one met the Nihangs at Hola Mohalla, and year three met the elders' army they trace themselves to. Today is the procession itself, and what it's announcing.
screen: `A KETTLE DRUM, SLOW AND HEAVY.` → `A TALL FLAG ON A POLE.` → `RIDERS IN DEEP BLUE.`

segments.voice: A dal is an army, a host, a band that moves together. The Nihang dals are the orders of Nihangs, each with its own leader, camps and customs, and each keeping the martial life of the old Khalsa riders. There is more than one, and they don't all do everything the same way. The drum is the nagara, and in a Nihang procession it goes in front. Tradition says the Gurus' court had its own war drum, and that beating it was a way of saying: this is a sovereign people, and it is here. When a Nihang dal moves today, the nagara still goes first. A salok of Bhagat Kabir in the Guru Granth Sahib gives the drum a meaning. In paraphrase: the drum beats in the sky of the mind, and the aim is struck. The true hero is the one who fights for deen, who may be cut apart piece by piece and still never leaves the field. Deen is a word some readers render as the faith, and some as the helpless. The drum is inside first; the battle is first a battle of the mind; and the hero stays, whatever it costs. That's what the blue army says it keeps: the outward life of the old riders, horses, weapons, the drum, and the inward reason for it. Some Nihang customs differ from the code you read in the last block. Sikhs hold a range of views about that, and some honor the dals as living memory of the Khalsa's hardest years. This path describes what they keep, and leaves the rest to the panth.

1309.title: Nihang speech
1309.hook: Nihangs speak in bold, playful coded phrases, like calling one Sikh a hundred and twenty-five thousand
1309.howItsDone: Nihangs use a distinctive speech, sometimes called Khalsa bole, with bold and playful names for everyday things; a single Nihang may call himself sava lakh, a hundred and twenty-five thousand.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Nihang dals, the nagara in front and Kabir's hero who never leaves the field. Your line was the blue army. Today, how the riders talk.

A lone rider comes into a village and someone asks how many are with him. He grins and says: a whole army. He's alone, and he isn't lying, not by his own way of speaking. Families do a small version of this. A dented old car gets called the limo. A sandwich at midnight is the feast. A kid scared of the dark is the brave one. The names aren't mistakes; they're a way of standing up straight. This week brought the shrine keepers, the scholars, the servers and the riders. It closes with the riders' language.
screen: `A LONE RIDER: A WHOLE ARMY.` → `THE DENTED CAR IS THE LIMO.` → `NAMES THAT STAND UP STRAIGHT.`

segments.voice: Nihangs have their own way of talking, sometimes called Khalsa bole, the Khalsa's speech, full of bold, playful names for ordinary things. Tradition says it grew up in the hard years, among riders who had very little, and it turned want into plenty with a word. A plain meal can get a grand name; danger gets a joke for a name. One well-worn example is the one in today's hook. A single Nihang may call himself sava lakh. Lakh means a hundred thousand; sava means one and a quarter. So one Sikh is a hundred and twenty-five thousand. The phrase comes from a saying tradition puts in Guru Gobind Singh's mouth, in paraphrase: I will make sparrows strike down hawks, and set one to fight a hundred and twenty-five thousand; only then will I be called Gobind Singh. The speech isn't a boast about strength. It's a refusal to feel small. If you're one, and there are many against you, it says: one is enough. The Guru Granth Sahib keeps that boldness in balance. In a salok of Guru Tegh Bahadur, in paraphrase: the one who frightens no one, and is frightened of no one, call that one wise. Read the two together. The bold name is for not being afraid, never for making someone else afraid. A Nihang calling himself an army is standing up straight, not standing over anyone. And notice the play in it: Nihang speech is funny on purpose, and courage with a smile on it is harder to crush.
screen: `KHALSA BOLE: THE RIDERS' SPEECH.` · `SAVA LAKH: ONE AS AN ARMY.` · `FEAR NO ONE, FRIGHTEN NO ONE.` · `COURAGE WITH A SMILE ON IT.` · then, large: `ONE IS ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Think of one place where you feel outnumbered, a meeting, a family argument, a task too big for one person, and give yourself a bold, playful name for it, the way a rider would. Then let Guru Tegh Bahadur's salok ride the breath: in, frighten no one; out, fear no one.

Your line: one is enough. Bold, but never standing over anyone. A week of streams, done.
